stories.h: EU AI Act amendments defer and clarify obligations
stories.s: Regulators’ push to defer and clarify obligations signals a broader shift toward clearer, enforceable rules for AI deployment that will ripple through funding, governance programs, and enterprise practices.
b: NSF announced the first awards to advance AI and cybersecurity education and workforce development through CyberAICorps Scholarship for Service Program (NSF.gov)
Army is launching AI-powered, commercial-facing DevSecOps platform (GovCIO Media & Research)
Cornerstone University launches President's AI Advisory Board to lead the future of Christian higher education (Cornerstone University)
EIN News reports on a Human AI Governance Operating System Puts Humans in Charge (EIN News)
body: The headline EU AI Act amendments defer and clarify obligations anchors a broader policy and governance discussion reflected across a set of related AI coverage. Across outlets, the conversation spans how institutions fund AI education, how governments shape compliance expectations, and how enterprises adopt governance tools to manage risk as AI use expands.

According to the National Science Foundation (NSF.gov), the agency has announced the first awards to advance AI and cybersecurity education and workforce development through the CyberAICorps Scholarship for Service Program, signaling continued emphasis on building a skilled AI workforce within the public and private sectors.

The coverage also notes military and defense-adjacent uptake of AI tools in enterprise-facing contexts. GovCIO Media & Research reports that the Army is launching an AI-powered, commercial-facing DevSecOps platform, reflecting ongoing interest in integrating AI into secure, scalable software pipelines.

In higher education, Cornerstone University announced the formation of a President's AI Advisory Board to lead the future of Christian higher education, a move highlighted by Cornerstone University as part of its strategic AI planning.

Rounding out the set, EIN News discusses governance-oriented AI framing, publishing a piece on a Humans-in-Charge approach via a Human AI Governance Operating System, illustrating ongoing debates about how human oversight fits into AI decision-making.

Beyond these, other items in the provided coverage touch on the economics, literacy, and practical deployment of AI: CEPR’s The AI premium, the World Economic Forum’s AI empathy gap, Chain Store Age’s survey on AI costs forcing strategic shifts, and OpenAI’s field report on scientists using AI coding agents to modernize scientific computing, respectively noted by OpenAI, CEPR, WEF, Chain Store Age, and OpenAI.
srcTitles: Scientific computing in the age of agentic AI

stories.h: Gemini API managed agents default to 3.6 Flash with environment hooks
stories.s: This update formalizes safer, cost-aware autonomous workflows and widens access for experimentation by enabling new safety and governance features in managed agents.
b: Gemini 3.6 Flash is now the default for Gemini API Managed Agents.
Environment hooks let you block, lint, or audit tool calls inside the sandbox via a configurable setup (e.g., .agents/hooks.json).
Budget controls, scheduled triggers, and free tier access are now available for managed agents.
To cap resource use, max_total_tokens can be set in agent_config; when reached, execution pauses with status “incomplete” and the state can be resumed later.
body: Google’s blog post on Gemini API Managed Agents announces that Gemini 3.6 Flash is now the default for managed agents, building on prior updates that introduced background tasks and remote server integrations.

A key upgrade is the introduction of environment hooks, which allow developers to run pre-tool and post-tool execution scripts inside the agent’s sandbox. The documentation notes that you can define hooks in a file like .agents/hooks.json and tailor actions for specific tools or events.

The post also highlights new governance features such as budget controls and scheduled triggers, along with free tier access for projects without active billing, making it easier to experiment with agentic workflows.

Crucially, the system supports token budgeting via max_total_tokens in agent_config. If the limit is hit, execution pauses and returns an incomplete status, preserving the environment so you can resume with a new budget and a previous_interaction_id. The update also reinforces the ability to explicitly select models through agent_config.model, including options like gemini-3.5-flash-lite.
srcTitles: Gemini API Managed Agents: 3.6 Flash, hooks, and more

stories.h: 5 ways to host the ultimate dinner party with Google Search
stories.s: Google’s AI Search tools could change how people plan real‑world gatherings, potentially increasing reliance on search‑driven planning and connected apps for events and entertaining.
b: AI features help visualize tablescapes and design custom menus
AI Mode can brainstorm recipes, find drink pairings, and curate music playlists that sync with apps
AI Mode can generate a printable menu and connect with Canva for design tasks
Prominent recipe results in Search show images and details like creator name, recipe ratings, and number of ingredients
body: Google’s latest AI features in Search aim to simplify dinner‑party planning by enabling users to visualize tablescapes, design menus, brainstorm recipes, locate drink pairings, and curate playlists that sync with preferred apps. The update focuses on helping you plan not just what to cook, but how to present and enjoy the overall experience.

Users can leverage Nano Banana in AI Mode to visualize how a table could look, while AI Mode helps brainstorm menu options and suggest drinks that complement chosen dishes. The AI tools are designed to streamline creative decisions, from theme to dish selection, so hosts can focus on guest experience.

Once decisions are made, AI Mode can generate a printable menu or shareable design, and it can connect with Canva to support on‑the‑fly design tasks as part of the planning flow. In addition, AI‑driven recipe results include richer details at the top of responses—images plus data such as the recipe creator’s name, ratings, and ingredient counts.

The article also notes that you can tie searches to your existing app ecosystem, for example by saving a playlist to YouTube Music or generating menu visuals you can print or share with guests, illustrating a broader push to make Google Search a planning hub for real‑world activities.

College students are highlighted as a demographic trending toward using these tools to remix dorm room spaces, with Google pointing to Search trends as evidence of growing interest in offline, real‑world planning.
srcTitles: 5 ways to host the ultimate dinner party with Google Search

stories.h: Samsung chip workers jump ship to SK Hynix after bigger bonuses
stories.s: The exodus signals a high-stakes talent war that could determine who leads AI memory chips and how quickly supply and pricing shift for AI accelerators.
b: SK Hynix is paying about $476,000 per employee this year, mostly in cash, to lure talent from Samsung
Samsung’s bonuses by division vary: memory division about $400,000 per employee vs. foundry division about $135,000
81.5% of employees in Samsung’s foundry division reportedly want to move to another company within two years, and more than 200 union members left for SK Hynix over the past four months

In H1 2026 SK Hynix added 2,152 employees to staff the expansion, and both firms topped $1 trillion in market value in May, with SK Hynix briefly dethroning Samsung as Korea’s most valuable company in June
body: MIT Technology Review reports that Samsung’s chip workers are jumping ship to SK Hynix as the AI hardware boom fuels a fierce talent war. Lee, an engineer in Samsung’s semiconductor division, describes coworkers applying to SK Hynix and says his team lead tells them to jump ship to SK Hynix, a message that has spread through the office as workers seek better pay and prospects.

The report notes that Samsung struck a deal in May to pay out 10.5% of the semiconductor division’s operating profits to employees as bonuses for 10 years, mostly in stock that vests over three years. In contrast, SK Hynix is paying a much larger upfront package: roughly $476,000 per employee this year, mostly in cash, a figure that dwarfs Samsung’s payouts. Within Samsung, bonuses vary by division: the memory division pays about $400,000 per employee this year, while the foundry division pays roughly $135,000.

Labor dynamics are central to the tale. Samsung’s labor union talks have yielded gains in other areas, but workers say the discrepancy in bonuses helps explain the defections. The Samsung labor union chief, Choi Seung-ho, has said that more than 200 members have left for SK Hynix in the past four months, and a June survey reported that 81.5% of foundry division employees want to move to another company within two years. Some employees also discuss their plans on Blind, an anonymous workplace forum, underscoring a broad morale challenge at Samsung’s chip plants.

The broader market context adds pressure to this talent war. MIT Technology Review notes that SK Hynix now leads the global market for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips, a technology central to AI accelerators, while Samsung has been scrambling to catch up. Both companies topped $1 trillion in market value in May, and SK Hynix briefly dethroned Samsung as Korea’s most valuable company in June. To staff expansion tied to this growth, SK Hynix reported adding 2,152 employees in the first half of 2026. In parallel, the AI spending boom and China’s progress in advanced chipmaking have fed a stock-market reaction: Bloomberg, via Techmeme, reported that South Korea’s KOSPI fell more than 11%, with Samsung down around 11% and SK Hynix down about 12%.

What happens next could reshape the AI hardware supply chain. MIT Technology Review frames the outcome as a race to dominate the next generation of HBMs, with the winner potentially locking in talent, boosting production capacity, and influencing pricing as demand for AI chips remains volatile.
srcTitles: Samsung’s chip workers are jumping ship to rival SK Hynix

stories.h: U.S. and UAE form bilateral AI task force to advance military AI development
stories.s: The move formalizes bilateral military AI collaboration and governance, signaling a coordinated push that could affect regional security, interoperability, and AI policy in a tense security landscape.
b: CENTCOM announced the US-UAE bilateral military AI task force, per Breaking Defense.
An Anadolu Ajansı report and other outlets describe it as a bilateral AI task force in the Middle East.
The coverage includes DefenseScoop and Middle East Monitor citing the joint effort and its aims to advance military AI development.
Yemen Online highlights that this may be the first bilateral military AI task force in the Middle East.
body: Multiple outlets report that the United States and the United Arab Emirates have formed a bilateral military AI task force aimed at advancing AI development in a defense context. The announcements reflect a growing emphasis on coordinating AI capabilities between allied nations in the security sphere.

Breaking Defense cites CENTCOM as the source of the announcement, noting that the task force represents an official U.S. military push to organize and oversee joint AI efforts with an ally in the region.

Other outlets—Anadolu Agency, Middle East Monitor, DefenseScoop, and Yemen Online—reiterate the bilateral nature of the initiative and frame it as a formal mechanism for collaboration on military AI, rather than a purely bilateral research program.

Yemen Online goes further to describe it as the first bilateral military AI task force in the Middle East, underscoring the regional significance of the partnership and its potential implications for interoperability and governance in AI-enabled defense capabilities.

stories.h: Steven Spielberg’s A.I. Artificial Intelligence turns 25 and remains unsettling
stories.s: The film’s enduring questions about machine autonomy and ethics shape how audiences, researchers, and policymakers think about real-world AI risks and governance.
b: 25th anniversary of Steven Spielberg’s A.I. Artificial Intelligence is being highlighted by coverage from The Independent and The Conversation.
The Conversation’s piece is titled “A.I. at 25: the Spielberg film that feels more unsettling than ever.”
Both outlets use the milestone to revisit themes of AI autonomy, ethics, and human–technology relationships that stay relevant to current AI debates.
body: The Independent marks the 25th anniversary of Steven Spielberg’s A.I. Artificial Intelligence, noting why the film still feels unsettling today. The piece uses the milestone to discuss the film’s ongoing resonance with audiences as AI technologies advance.

The Conversation also weighs in on the anniversary, framing it as a moment to reflect on the Spielberg film’s themes and their relevance in contemporary AI discourse. The Conversation’s take is framed around how the film’s questions about artificial sentience and human control continue to provoke unease.

Both outlets connect the film’s exploration of machine autonomy, ethics, and the complex relationship between humans and technology to the broader, real‑world conversations around AI safety, governance, and public perception.

Overall, the anniversary serves as a cultural touchstone for examining how narratives about AI influence policy debates, research priorities, and public attitudes toward increasingly capable intelligent systems.
srcTitles: Steven Spielberg’s A.I. Artificial Intelligence turns 25. Here’s why the movie still feels unsettling today
